extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism; scholars of 19th-century American literature
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative principles and stylistic standards for assessing 19th-century poetry and narrative fiction (theory vs practice, rhythm, sound devices, plot plausibility, characterization), illustrated through discussion of Lanier, Whitman, Hawthorne, and Lydia Maria Child.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's educated love of beauty / ear appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: "For the artist in verse there is no law; the perception and love of beauty constitute the whole outfit ... In all cases the appeal is, the ear; but the ear should for that purpose be educated up to the highest possible plane of culture."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The primary standard for verse is sensitivity to beauty and an appeal to sound; theoretical rules are subordinate hints intended to enlarge perception and cultivate the ear. Emphasizes cultivation of musical sensibility over rigid prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accent-based meter (count by accents, not syllables)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier (following Coleridge's principle) associates modern English verse with counting by accents rather than by syllables.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle explains the transition from strict measured verse to freer modern rhythms and links nursery rhymes/folk songs with modern prosody; use accentual rather than strictly syllabic metrics when aiming for modern rhythmic freedom.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musicality: beat, cadence, and rhythmic variety
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry should demonstrate a 'wonderful beat and cadence' — e.g., 'a line of a dozen syllables mating with a line of a single syllable' — producing satisfying movement and variety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for variety in line-lengths and cadences to create musical movement; rhythmic juxtaposition can be as effective as formal meter. Examples: Mother Goose rhythms, plantation 'patting Juba', and Lanier's marsh hymns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Orchestration / distribution of sound (antiphonal effects)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's experience as a musician gave him 'an ear for the distribution of instruments,' favoring antiphonal effects, answers, echoes, and compensating notes in poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the interplay of voices/lines and the use of call-and-response or echoing structures to enrich texture; treat elements of a poem like instruments in an ensemble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of simple folk-song sound devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Simple devices of sound familiar in nursery songs and folk tunes can produce lyrical effects like Shakespeare's, often indistinguishable from 'Mother Goose' in their lyricism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ elementary sound devices (repetition, simple rhythms, nursery-song patterns) deliberately to achieve powerful lyrical effects rather than dismissing them as lowly or unsophisticated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theory versus practice: theories are hints, not laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's own statement that his propositions are 'hints only, and not laws' and that poetry written upon theory alone would be hindered rather than helped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use theoretical systems as suggestive tools to enlarge perception; avoid producing poetry that mechanically follows theory at the cost of organic artistic feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer craft-based criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Effective criticism should be like that 'a sculptor receives from a brother sculptor,' focusing on craft and internal standards rather than consumer or artisan viewpoints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should be informed, craft-aware, and generous in discernment; examples include Lanier's nuanced appraisals (e.g., of Swinburne and Morris) which balance praise for craft with substantive judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity and avoidance of pose / self-consciousness
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier criticizes Whitman for 'attitudinizing and self-consciousness...everywhere posing' and calls such affectation 'the extreme of sophistication in writing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Value sincerity and authentic voice; be wary of calculated poses or self-conscious attempts to appear 'rough' or 'barbaric' that mask artifice rather than convey genuine feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not subject creative work to partial criticism; read the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Hawthorne 'always disliked ... to have anything criticised until the whole had been heard.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate a work only after experiencing it in full; partial readings can mislead critics and deprive authors of the cumulative effects intended by structure and pacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot plausibility and sound execution in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of 'Hobomok' as 'very crude in execution, very improbable in plot' — plotting and workmanship are essential measures of a novel's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess narrative coherence and plausibility; improbable plot turns and poor execution weaken a work even if other qualities are present.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local coloring and earnestness can redeem flaws
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Hobomok' is 'redeemed only by a certain earnestness which carries the reader along, and by a sincere attempt after local coloring.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authentic local detail and evident earnestness of purpose can compensate for technical weaknesses; emphasize credible setting and heartfelt engagement when craft is imperfect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative energy: vigor, variety, picturesque grouping, animation of style
rubrics_metrics.description: Praise for 'The Rebels' for having 'more vigor, more variety, more picturesque grouping, and more animation of style.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate fiction on its dynamism — energetic pacing, varied scenes, vivid grouping of characters/events, and lively stylistic tone contribute to reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid lazy over-tragic devices (killing characters for convenience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author notes a young-writer tendency to 'over-tragic' solutions, finding it 'so much easier to kill off superfluous characters than to do anything else with them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticize gratuitous or convenient deaths as signs of weak plotting; develop or repurpose characters rather than removing them as an escape from narrative difficulty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and restraint; avoid spasmodic phrases and fancies pressed too hard
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's marsh hymn contains 'inequalities, little spasmodic phrases here and there, or fancies pressed too hard,' even while containing lines not excelled by Keats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Watch for unevenness and overwrought passages; aim for balance so that brilliant lines do not sit alongside jarring or forced phrases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of themes and treatment guided by substantive beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Lanier's later prose 'takes up the substantiate, — the selection of themes, treatment of accessories, and the like,' as part of a philosophy of formal and substantial beauty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge works also by their thematic choices and treatments — select subjects and accessory details that coherently serve the work's conception of beauty and artistic aims.
